articles.title: Somalis, roiled by famine and climate displacement, brace for El Niño
articles.summary: Thousands of people in Somalia have already left their villages to seek refuge in bigger cities in the Horn of Africa amid a hunger crisis. Many are desperat...
articles.body:
Thousands of Somalis are fleeing their villages due to a hunger crisis exacerbated by drought and low crop yields, with many facing malnutrition and food shortages.

The looming El Nino weather phenomenon is expected to bring fresh floods to Somalia, further worsening the already dire situation for displaced people, with international support plummeting by 88% compared to the previous year.

Lack of funding for aid work, rising fuel and food prices, and the potential spread of diseases like cholera and malaria pose additional challenges for response teams and vulnerable populations in Somalia as they brace for the impact of El Nino.

Thousands of people in Somalia have already left their villages to seek refuge in bigger cities in the Horn of Africa amid a hunger crisis.

Many are desperate after months of drought and a harvest that only made about 20% of average yields.

Most Somalis are pastoralists, relying on their herds to survive. But many cows, sheep and goats have died in the ongoing drought.

The Somali government declared a food emergency last November and the situation improved slightly.

But many herders and farmers are still trying to recover from a drought followed by heavy flooding in 2022 and 2023. Now, they face the same scenario all over again.

After months of drought, fresh floods are forecast once El Niño reverses the traditional arid conditions.

The World Meteorological Organization expects this year's El Niño in October - and all prognoses are dire. A very powerful El Niño may significantly shift rainfall and temperature patterns worldwide and fuel extreme weather, the UN agency says.

"El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up. Sea surface temperatures are rising, temperatures keep climbing, and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather," UN Secretary-General António Guterres said in early September.

Somalia is one of the countries where climate related displacement is not a future threat but a painful reality.

It means cities including Mogadishu or Baidoa see hundreds of new arrivals, building provisional shelters that are unlikely to withstand heavy rain.

And one in every two children screened in displacement sites in Baidoa is acutely malnourished, according to aid organization Doctors Without Borders (MSF). One in every four is severely malnourished.

"What we are seeing is shocking and far beyond the threshold of an extremely critical emergency," MSF's project coordinator in Somalia, Allar Ali, said during a recent briefing in Nairobi.

"The world cannot wait for a famine declaration before acting," says Ali. "Action is needed now to prevent loss of lives."

But not enough money is available. The malnutrition situation has already reached the levels of 2022, MSF says. Some 6 million people in Somalia — about one in three — faces food shortages.

Among them, nearly 1.9 million people are in an emergency and need urgent help.

But international support has plummeted by 88% compared with 2022.

"These funding cuts are blocking access to health care, they are leading to the closure of nutrition services, they are pushing all the vital things that children need – water, education, protection – further and further away," says James Elder, spokesman for the UN children's fund UNICEF.

"And as always, it is the children who pay the price," he told dpa.

Some 50 health care centres have been forced to close due to such cuts, says Sarah Easter, emergency communication officer for Care in Germany.

The aid organization has also been forced to halt many projects since the end of May due to a lack of funding.

The centres treated malnourished children, as well as youngsters suffering from malaria or diarrhoeal diseases.

This is not an isolated case. "If the trend continues until the end of the year, more than 630 will be closed," she told dpa. "This is really a catastrophe, especially in view of El Niño."

Stagnant water means contaminated water and lots of mosquitoes. In such situations, diseases such as cholera spread rapidly. Malaria is also widespread.

Children who are already weak and malnourished are at the greatest risk.

"In the camps I visited in Mogadishu, there are no longer any health centres, there is no more food distribution, there is no more water distribution, there is no more cash aid. There are no longer any projects that are for women and girls who have experienced violence," Easter says.

Somalis are not only suffering from the lack of funding for aid work. The war in Iran and the shipping halt in the vital Hormuz Strait means fuel and food prices are rising.

"A sack of rice has become at least 1.5 times more expensive,", Easter says. "Humanitarian aid has also become incredibly more expensive."

Peanut paste, given to malnourished children under 5 years, used to cost $139 for a box containing 500 packs. It now costs $200, Easter says. "And we expect it to go up even further."

She fears what is to come. Response teams are struggling, though they will be sorely needed if El Nino brings flooding, as is forecast.

The Somali Disaster Agency says it had helicopters in 2023 - the UN had helicopters that could fly food aid to affected areas and evacuations were also possible.

"Back then, they had 40 helicopters that flew non-stop, all day long," Easter says.

"This year, there are no helicopters, and only six boats out of the 60 they had last time, to reach people in flooded areas."

articles.title: From oratory to screen time, PM & teachers exchange notes
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: \"You need confidence and plenty of practice.\" That was the public-speaking advice PM Narendra Modi received from a national award-winning t.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: "You need confidence and plenty of practice." That was the public-speaking advice PM Narendra Modi received from a national award-winning teacher during an interaction that moved from a joke about his "aura" to screen addiction, drug abuse and the need to preserve childhood.Modi had asked the teacher what she would advise him if he were her student and wanted to become a good orator. After her tip, she said, "Sorry, sir. Seeing your aura, my aura went down a little."The interaction with National Teachers Award winners was held at Modi's Lok Kalyan Marg residence Friday, the eve of Teachers' Day.One teacher said she was teaching children how to conduct interviews like journalists. Students had begun questioning their parents at home: "Why was this food cooked? Why was it cooked this way? Who made the decision? How much was spent?" She added, "All the children in my school now want to become reporters."Modi asked teachers not to judge children only by their academic performance. A child might struggle with studies but possess another ability, he said. Modi said children were naturally curious and teachers should nurture and guide that curiosity.Calling excessive screen time a form of addiction, the PM said children could be drawn away from phones by making them develop an interest in sports - "not video games, but playing on the field" - and creative activities. Teachers should speak to parents about how much time their kids spent on screens.On drug abuse, Modi said the problem was not confined to large cities and universities. Teachers must spread awareness, watch out for behavioural changes, and help those affected.When a teacher spoke about educating women on breast cancer, Modi referred to a similar awareness campaign in Varanasi, his Lok Sabha constituency. He said more women were now coming forward for check-ups and that a Guinness World Record had been set for the highest number of screenings in a day.Referring to National Education Policy, the PM urged teachers to take learning beyond classrooms. Children should be connected with real-world skills and taught values like the dignity of labour."The biggest contribution teachers can make is to keep childhood alive in students," the PM added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Iraq completes investigation into thousands of ISIS detainees formerly held in Syria
articles.summary: The US-backed Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) had been holding them until the SDF and Syrian government agreed to integrate, at which time US Central Command...
articles.body:
Iraq has completed an investigation into around 5,700 ISIS detainees transferred from Syria, with some suspects identified as top-ranking figures involved in international crimes.

Some of the ISIS members will now return to their home countries, including Syria, Turkey, and others, after being held in camps and facilities in Syria for seven years.

Over 20,000 Iraqi nationals have been rehabilitated after returning from Syria's al-Hol camp, with many countries refusing to take back their ISIS members.

The US-backed Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) had been holding them until the SDF and Syrian government agreed to integrate, at which time US Central Command decided to facilitate a mass transfer.

Iraq says it has completed an investigation into around 5,700 ISIS detainees who were transferred from Syria earlier this year.

The ISIS detainees are mostly men who had been held in around two dozen detention facilities in eastern Syria since 2019. The US-backed Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) had been holding them until the SDF and Syrian government agreed to integrate, at which time US Central Command decided to facilitate a mass transfer to Iraq.

Now Iraq says it has investigated most of these people. It is not clear precisely how many will be put on trial in Iraq or remain in detention.

ISIS was mostly defeated in Syria in 2019, at which point around 50-80,000 ISIS members ended up detained in Syria by the SDF. Most of the detainees were women and children. However, several thousand of them were men, considered to be more dangerous than the women and children.

A report at Al-Arabiya that is based on an AFP report notes that "the cases will now proceed to trial, while more than 450 Syrians will be released and handed over to their country. Iraq's Supreme Judicial Council said it concluded 'the interrogation phase'of the 5,704 ISIS suspects who were brought from northeast Syria, and referred them to trial."

Some detainees to return to home countries

This matters because some of these ISIS members will now return to their home countries such as Syria, Turkey and other places. The ISIS members held in camps and facilities in Syria had come from 60 countries. The international community, including around 80 countries, backed the anti-ISIS coalition. However, they didn't create any kind of international court to charge the ISIS members. Instead, the members were left in limbo for seven years.

The Al-Arabia report notes that "the investigations led to identifying several ISIS commanders, including top-ranking figures, who were involved in 'crimes at the international level,' according to the council." It added that at least six suspects are documented to have been involved in the genocide against the Yazidi minority in Iraq.

In 2014, ISIS overran the Yazidi areas of Iraq's Sinjar and began to systematically murder the Yazidis. It also kidnapped thousands of women and children and sold them into slavery. This helped galvanize the international community to fight ISIS.

In general, the Yazidis have not received justice, and most ISIS members appear to have escaped having to actually stand trial. Some died in the war. Many thousands of Yazidis remain missing. Over the last decade, some Yazidi women and children have continued to be found in Syria and other places.

The New Region reported that "over 20,000 Iraqis rehabilitated from al-Hol camp." The report comes from Iraq's government.

"Iraq's migration ministry on Saturday said over 20,000 Iraqi nationals have been rehabilitated after returning from Syria's notorious al-Hol camp," the report added. The report noted that "the Iraqi detainees were transferred to al-Jadaa camp, a major government-run rehabilitation and integration center south of Mosul."

Iraq has worked hard to repatriate its people over the last year. However, many countries have refused to take back their ISIS members. Australia, for instance, was reluctant to take back women and children who had been in Al-Hol in Syria.

articles.title: Aadhaar for rest, but babus resist link for CGHS
articles.summary: India News: Over 3,100 DBT schemes and 360 public services use Aadhaar-based authentication. Yet the bureaucracy that demands Aadhaar from citizens, often the poo.
articles.body: Over 3,100 DBT schemes and 360 public services use Aadhaar-based authentication. Yet the bureaucracy that demands Aadhaar from citizens, often the poorest, has resisted linking their own Central Govt Health Scheme cards to Aadhaar.CGHS beneficiaries include serving and retired central govt employees and family members, sitting and former MPs, sitting and retired judges of SC and HCs, accredited journalists in DelhiAadhaar linking "has helped state ensure targeted, transparent and leak-proof delivery while eliminating duplicate and ineligible beneficiaries," said PIB. However, bureaucrats aren't walking the talk.What’s must for poor is voluntary for babusThere is no annual verification to weed out dead pensioners or their dependents who might have become ineligible. Two other central govt health schemes, the Ex-Servicemen Contributory Health Scheme and the railway health scheme, have made it mandatory to link Aadhaar.Govt has issued office memoranda making Aadhaar linking mandatory several times starting from June 2015, but has had to withdraw it in the face of stiff resistance from its employees.The last such withdrawal happened in July 2024 when the govt was forced to keep the directive to link CGHS beneficiary ID with Ayushman Bharat Health account ID (ABHA ID), created using Aadhaar, “in abeyance till further orders”.The linkage has since been made voluntary for central govt employees, though it is mandatory for a poor woman to get Rs 300 as daily wage under the employment guarantee scheme.While Aadhaar has been mandated for “welfare schemes funded from the Consolidated Fund of India”, including many DBT sche-mes, babus have been arguing that CGHS is a contributory scheme and not a DBT scheme, despite 90% of spending on the scheme coming from the Consolidated Fund of India. Their contributions amount to a tiny part of the annual expenditure on the scheme.CGHS incidentally has a higher per capita expenditure when compared to ECHS and the railway health scheme. It would be even higher if deceased beneficiaries and ineligible dependents were weeded out. Pensioner cards made at the start of computerisation of CGHS in 2005 remain active in the system without any checks increasing the chances of fraud and misuse of such cards.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: CBI FIR against Subhash Chandra in alleged Rs 1,322cr LIC Housing Finance fraud
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: CBI has filed an FIR against Essel Group Chairman Subhash Chandra and some other individuals for allegedly defrauding LICHFL (LIC Housing F.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: CBI has filed an FIR against Essel Group Chairman Subhash Chandra and some other individuals for allegedly defrauding LICHFL (LIC Housing Finance Ltd) of Rs 1,322 crore between 2018 and 2026. LICHFL alleged that Chandra had submitted a 'net worth certificate' of Rs 59,113 crore in 2018 while availing credit facilities but in 2024 stated that his net worth was just Rs 31.7 crore. The FIR was registered on a complaint filed by LICHFL on Aug 31.According to the FIR, LICHFL had sanctioned two loan facilities totalling Rs 980 crore to four companies. A Rs 500-crore facility was sanctioned to Vasant Sagar Properties Pvt Ltd and Pan India Infraprojects Pvt Ltd, while another Rs 480 crore was given to Digital Subscriber Management and Consultancy Services Pvt Ltd and Spirit Infrapower and Multiventures Pvt Ltd.Chandra denied possessing net worth stated in certificatesBoth facilities were backed by personal guarantees furnished by Essel Group chairman Subhash Chandra. The complaint alleged that the loans were sanctioned on the basis of net-worth certificates submitted on behalf of Chandra. One certificate, issued in March 2018, allegedly showed his net worth at $6,197.6 million, equivalent to around Rs 59,113 crore, as of March 31, 2017. Another certificate put his net worth at Rs 40,562 crore.However, the complaint stated, during the subsequent insolvency proceedings, Subhash Chandra had denied possessing the net worth reflected in the certificates. He allegedly stated that his net worth in 2024 was Rs 31.79 crore and that even in 2017-18 it had not exceeded Rs 40,000 crore.The outstanding amount against the Vasant Sagar facility was stated to be Rs 570.50 crore, while Rs 507.25 crore was outstanding against the Digital Subscriber facility.LICHFL alleged that Chandra, in collusion with the borrower companies and their directors, induced the housing finance company to release the funds by submitting false and inflated documents. It further alleged that the funds were subsequently misappropriated and assets were stripped to frustrate recovery efforts.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: FBI's fifth 'Most Wanted Fraudster' captured after alleged SNAP scam suspect arrested in India
articles.summary: Manjit Singh Bedi was arrested in India after allegedly fleeing the U.S. to escape SNAP benefits fraud charges tied to a $600,000 EBT scheme.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: The FBI's Most Wanted Fraudsters initiative notched its fifth arrest in just three months after authorities in India arrested Manjit Singh Bedi on Friday, with the bureau now working to return the alleged SNAP benefits fraud suspect to the United States, Fox News Digital has learned. The FBI worked with Indian authorities to secure Bedi's arrest and is actively working to return him to the U.S. to face charges, according to the bureau. Bedi's arrest marks the fifth under the FBI's Most Wanted Fraudsters initiative, which targets fugitives accused of major financial crimes. Launched in June, the initiative has led to the arrests of five fugitives whom the FBI says are collectively accused of more than $2 billion in alleged fraud after spending nearly 4,000 combined days on the run. FBI NABS ALLEGED $547M MEDICARE FRAUD FUGITIVE OVERSEAS, THIRD CAPTURE FROM 'MOST WANTED FRAUDSTERS' LIST FBI officials say the latest arrest underscores the bureau's effort to pursue alleged fraudsters who fled overseas in an attempt to evade prosecution. "Five Most Wanted Fraudsters captured in just three months is a historic success for this initiative," FBI Director Kash Patel told Fox News Digital. Patel said the five suspects are allegedly responsible for more than $2 billion in fraud and spent nearly 4,000 combined days on the run before their arrests. "The days of taking advantage of American taxpayers without consequence are over," Patel said. Federal investigators allege Bedi defrauded the U.S. government out of at least $600,000 through a Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) fraud scheme between March 2024 and June 2025, while operating an Asian grocery store in Tacoma, Washington. EXCLUSIVE: FBI ADDS ALLEGED COVID FRAUDSTER ACCUSED OF TAKING $5M FROM KIDS' MEAL PROGRAM TO MOST WANTED LIST According to the FBI, Bedi allegedly swiped SNAP recipients' Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) cards, gave them cash instead of eligible food purchases and kept roughly half of the benefits for himself. After being indicted on wire fraud and SNAP benefits fraud charges, Bedi was ordered to surrender his passport and remain in Washington state while awaiting court proceedings, according to the FBI. Investigators allege he instead drove across the Canadian border before fleeing to India. A federal arrest warrant charging him with violating the conditions of his release was issued on May 21, 2026. The FBI had offered a reward of up to $150,000 for information leading to Bedi's arrest and conviction. The bureau said the naturalized U.S. citizen was believed to be living in India before his arrest. "As this arrest in India shows, the Justice Department's reach extends to every corner of the planet," Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division told Fox News Digital. The FBI said it is working to return Bedi to the U.S. to face the pending charges.

articles.title: Limerick: Two-year-old boy dies after hit-and-run
articles.summary: The boy was taken to hospital with serious injuries but was later pronounced dead.
articles.body:
A two-year-old boy has died after being struck by a vehicle in County Limerick.

The collision, involving a Jeep and the child, happened in the Abbeycourt area of Rathkeale shortly before 16:00 BST on Saturday.

The boy was taken to University Hospital Limerick with serious injuries but was later pronounced dead.

Gardaí (Irish Police) said the vehicle involved did not remain at the scene.

A man in his 30s was later arrested at a different location on suspicion of driving under the influence of an intoxicant.

He was taken to a Garda Station in Co. Limerick to provide a blood/urine sample and was later released pending analysis of that test.

Gardaí say the investigation is ongoing.
